extraction.name: MMMU
extraction.description: MMMU is a benchmark consisting of 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, and focus on advanced perception and reasoning with domain-specific knowledge.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Questions were manually collected by a team of 50 college students (including coauthors) from various disciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, textbooks, and lecture materials. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoiding data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution. They were advised to select questions without immediately available answers. The process involved three stages: (1) selecting 30 subjects from six disciplines based on whether visual inputs are commonly adopted, (2) recruiting university students specializing in these majors to collect multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources or create new questions based on their expertise, (3) quality control through lexical overlap and URL similarity checks for duplicates, format and typo checking by co-authors, and categorizing problems into four difficulty levels (very easy, easy, medium, hard), with very easy problems excluded.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Quality control was performed through duplicate detection using lexical overlap and source URL similarity, followed by manual review. Format and typo checking was conducted by co-authors. Problems were categorized into difficulty levels, with approximately 10% classified as very easy being excluded from the benchmark. Error analysis was conducted on 150 randomly sampled error instances from GPT-4V's predictions, analyzed by expert annotators who identified root causes based on their knowledge and golden explanations.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 college students (including coauthors) from various disciplines and subjects, specializing in the 30 majors covered by the benchmark. For human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students were selected to represent experts in the corresponding 30 subjects (3 student experts per subject).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: OCR by MMOCR and captioning by LLaVA-1.5 were used to provide recognized text information to text-only LLMs for evaluation purposes, not for creating the dataset annotations.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases. The benchmark focuses on college-level subjects which might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. The selection of subjects was based on the principle that visual inputs should be commonly adopted, which ruled out subjects like law and linguistics.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI as there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and '90th percentile of skilled adults,' nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. The benchmark combines multiple-choice questions with concise open-ended questions to balance complexity and practicality. Approximately 10% of problems classified as very easy were excluded from the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark aims to monitor progress towards Expert AGI, which marks a critical milestone denoting AI systems that reach 'at least 90th percentile of skilled adults' in a broad range of tasks. This has significant implications for job displacement and economic disruption. The benchmark is designed to push the boundaries of what LMMs can achieve and prove instrumental in developing next-generation multimodal foundation models.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The benchmark is designed for evaluating multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It is used for zero-shot evaluation to assess the capability of models to generate accurate answers without fine-tuning. The benchmark is divided into a few-shot development set (5 questions per subject), a validation set (approximately 900 questions useful for hyperparameter selection), and a test set (10.5K questions).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Multi-stage data quality control including: (1) lexical overlap and source URL similarity to identify potential duplicates with manual review by authors, (2) format and typo checking by co-authors to ensure standardized format with necessary corrections, (3) categorization into four difficulty levels (very easy, easy, medium, hard) with exclusion of approximately 10% of problems classified as very easy

name.evidence: We introduce MMMU: a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning.

description.evidence: MMMU includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: To determine if an external image-to-text tool can enhance these LLMs' performance on MMMU, we deploy OCR by MMOCR or captioning by LLaVA-1.5 to provide the recognized text information to text-only LLMs.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI [57]... The selection is based on the principle that visual inputs should be commonly adopted in the subjects to provide valuable information. Through this principle, we rule out a few subjects like law and linguistics because it is difficult to find enough relevant multimodal problems in these subjects.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: MMMU, like any benchmark, has limitations despite its comprehensive nature... We shall caution that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI, as per the definition [57], because there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and '90th percentile of skilled adults,' nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle... To strike a balance between complexity and practicality, MMMU combines multiple-choice questions with concise open-ended questions, enabling the assessment of diverse subjects while addressing the challenges associated with evaluating open-ended responses... Approximately 10% of the problems, classified as very easy and not aligning with our design criteria due to their simplistic nature, are excluded from the benchmark.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: In the suggested taxonomy, Level 3, or Expert AGI, marks a critical milestone. It denotes an AI system that reaches 'at least 90th percentile of skilled adults' in a broad range of tasks, thus starting to achieve 'the substitution threshold for machine intelligence in lieu of human labor' for many industries, leading to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. Therefore, it is of both intellectual and societal importance to closely monitor the progress towards Expert AGI... Our aim with MMMU is to push the boundaries of what LMMs can achieve. We believe it will prove instrumental in developing next-generation multimodal foundation models and monitoring the progress towards Expert AGI.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We introduce MMMU: a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning... Our evaluation is conducted under a zero-shot setting to assess the capability of models to generate accurate answers without fine-tuning or few-shot demonstrations on our benchmark... MMMU, constituting 11.5K questions, is divided into a few-shot development set, a validation set, and a test set. The few-shot development set includes 5 questions per subject, and the validation set, useful for hyperparameter selection, contains approximately 900 questions, while the test set comprises 10.5K questions.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: To further control the quality of our data, we perform two steps of data cleaning. In the first stage, lexical overlap and source URL similarity are employed to identify potential duplicate problems. These suspected duplicates were then reviewed by the authors to identify and eliminate any duplications. The second stage involves distributing the problems among different co-authors for format and typo checking. This step requires authors to ensure adherence to a standardized format, undertaking necessary corrections where deviations are found. In the third and final stage, the authors categorize the problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of the problems, classified as very easy and not aligning with our design criteria due to their simplistic nature, are excluded from the benchmark.
